correctness.rationale: Strong pseudoperfectness forces \(\sigma(n)\ge2n\). This immediately eliminates \(p,p^2,p^3\), leaves only \(6\) in the \(pq\) shape, and leaves exactly \(12,18,20,28\) in the \(p^2q\) shape; complementary-pair subset sums retain only \(28\). For squarefree \(pqr\), the pair containing \(1\) is forced, and all seven nonempty choices among the other three pair sums are eliminated by the displayed Diophantine reductions. The proof covers every factorization shape with \(\Omega(n)\le3\), while \(6,28,36\) have explicit representations.

value.rationale: The class was introduced specifically as an intermediate rigidity notion between perfect and pseudoperfect numbers, and the newest dedicated paper studies structural restrictions. The theorem gives the exact first multiplicative-complexity boundary: below four prime factors counted with multiplicity, strong pseudoperfectness collapses to ordinary perfectness, while the first non-perfect example \(36\) attains four. This is a natural complete classification, not a chosen numerical slice, and it explains a visible feature of the canonical sequence.
